---
title: "Methodology"
---

How the comparisons are made, so they can be checked and reproduced.

## Same inputs

Inputs for each example are generated once in Julia with a fixed seed and written to
`data/<example>.npz`. All three implementations load that file.

## Same gradient

Every implementation computes the gradient of the same loss at the same point in
**Float64** and saves it to `benchmarks/grads/<example>_<impl>.npz`. Each example page
checks that

1. every gradient agrees with central finite differences on a few random components, and
2. all three gradients agree with each other (relative tolerance 1e-8).

A failing check fails the build, so a published page always shows matching gradients.

## Timing

- Everything runs in **Float64**, timing included, so the timed code is exactly the code
  whose gradient was checked. The laptop GPU used here has low Float64 throughput (as
  most consumer GPUs do), which slows every GPU column; relative comparisons between
  GPU columns are what matter.
- Compile time (first call) is reported separately from run time. It matters for JAX and
  Reactant, which compile a whole graph, and for Enzyme, which compiles on first call.
- Run time is the median of 10 calls after 2 warm-up calls. GPU work is synchronised
  inside the timed region (`CUDA.synchronize`, `jax.block_until_ready`).
- Problem size *N* is swept over several orders of magnitude so scaling is visible, not
  just one data point.
- Peak device memory is reported where the tool exposes it.
- Benchmarks run on an otherwise idle GPU (`make gpu-check` refuses to run otherwise).

## Fairness rules for the JAX column

The JAX code is what a competent JAX user would write, not a literal translation:

- `jax.jit` everything, donate buffers where it helps, and use `jax.checkpoint` where a
  practitioner would.
- Use the ecosystem's own tools where they exist: jax-md cell and neighbour lists,
  Optimistix for implicit differentiation, Diffrax for adaptive time stepping.
- Where JAX needs a static capacity (padding), size it from the data and handle overflow
  the way jax-md does, and report the padding overhead.
- Every example page has a **"Where JAX wins / what we did not do"** note.

## Hardware and software

Results on the published site were produced on an NVIDIA RTX 5000 Ada Generation Laptop
GPU (16 GB), Julia 1.12, Enzyme.jl 0.13, Reactant.jl 0.2, JAX 0.11 (CUDA 13). Exact
versions are pinned in `julia/Manifest.toml` and `python/uv.lock`.
